wstep: This card describes the NCHFP (University of Georgia) recipe for freezer lemon curd: a cream of egg yolks, eggs, butter and bottled lemon juice that can be frozen for up to 1 year.

akapity: 2 1/2 cups superfine sugar, 1/2 cup freshly grated lemon zest, 1 cup bottled lemon juice, 3/4 cup unsalted butter, chilled and cut into pieces of about 3/4 inch (about 1.9 cm), 7 large egg yolks and 4 large whole eggs.
If you have no superfine sugar, grind regular sugar for 1 minute in a grinder or food processor, let it settle and use it instead.
You need, among other things, a double boiler of at least 1 1/2 quarts, a strainer, a kitchen thermometer measuring at least up to 180 °F (about 82 °C) and freezer containers of 1 quart capacity.
Wash the freezer containers in warm, soapy water, rinse them well and dry them, and keep them covered or upside down on a clean surface until filling.
Mix the sugar with the zest and set aside for about 30 minutes; meanwhile measure the juice and prepare the chilled butter pieces.
Heat the water in the bottom pan until it boils gently; it must not boil vigorously or touch the bottom of the top pan.
In the top pan, beat the egg yolks and whole eggs thoroughly but lightly with a whisk, slowly whisk in the sugar and zest, then the lemon juice and the butter pieces.
Place the top pan over the boiling water, stir gently but continuously and cook until the mixture reaches 170 °F (about 77 °C); check the temperature with a thermometer.
Remove the pan from the heat and stir gently until the curd thickens, about 5 minutes.
Strain the curd through a strainer into a glass or stainless steel bowl, and discard the zest.
Cool the curd to room temperature, covering its surface with plastic wrap or covering the bowl so no skin forms.
Fill the curd into freezer containers, leave 1/2 inch (about 1.3 cm) headspace and freeze immediately.
Freeze at 0 °F (−18 °C) or lower.
To speed up freezing, set the freezer to −10 °F (about −23 °C) or lower about 24 hours in advance.
Do not overload the freezer: add only as much unfrozen food as will freeze within 24 hours.
Keep the freezer at 0 °F (−18 °C) or lower, because at higher temperatures food loses quality faster; keep a freezer thermometer in it and check it often.
According to the NCHFP, lemon curd can be kept in the freezer for up to 1 year without quality changes when thawed.
Use the oldest packages first.
Thaw the container in the refrigerator at 40 °F (about 4 °C) or lower for 24 hours before use.
Eat thawed lemon curd within 4 weeks.
Lime curd uses the same recipe: instead of the lemon juice and zest, use 1 cup bottled lime juice and 1/4 cup fresh lime zest.
Food is safe while it stays frozen, but once it thaws and warms above 40 °F (about 4 °C), bacteria present before freezing can start to multiply.
During a power outage keep the freezer closed: according to the FDA, a full freezer holds its temperature for about 48 hours, a half-full one for 24 hours.
When the power comes back, the FDA says that food which still contains ice crystals or is at 40 °F (about 4 °C) or below is safe to refreeze or cook; you cannot judge this by look or smell.
According to the NCHFP, food stays frozen longer if the freezer is full, unopened, in a cool place and well insulated; it can be covered with blankets, away from the compressor.
JarAtlas rule (cautious) after a freezer failure: throw away any package that has no ice crystals and is above 40 °F (about 4 °C), or that you cannot check.
The FDA also says to throw away perishable food that has been at room temperature for 2 hours or more, or 1 hour when it is above 90 °F (about 32 °C) outside.
